title: Writing: The First Information Technology
subtitle: The earliest writing wasn't poetry or history — it was receipts. And that unglamorous origin tells you exactly why writing changed the world.
hook: We imagine writing began with someone recording a great story or a law. It didn't. The world's earliest writing is mostly **accounting** — lists of grain, sheep, and taxes owed. That's a letdown until you realize *why*: once farming produced surplus (our last History lesson), someone had to track who stored what, who owed whom, and what the temple collected. Writing was invented to **manage information that had outgrown human memory.** It was civilization's first information technology — and every later leap, up to the internet, rhymes with it.

sections.heading: From tokens to tablets
sections.body:
In ancient Mesopotamia, traders first tracked goods with small clay **tokens** — one shape per commodity. As trade grew, they pressed the tokens' marks into clay tablets instead, then simplified those marks into symbols. By around **3400–3000 BCE** this became **cuneiform**: wedge-shaped signs pressed into clay. Egypt developed hieroglyphs, China its own script, Mesoamerica another — again, **independent invention**, echoing the pattern we saw with farming.

Crucially, early writing recorded *quantities and things*, not speech. Only later did symbols come to stand for **sounds**, at which point writing could capture anything language could — names, laws, stories, ideas.

sections.caption: Writing's origin is the same chain we started last lesson: surplus created records to keep, and the technology to keep them evolved from tokens to a full script.

sections.label: Why it was revolutionary
sections.body: Writing let information escape the limits of a single human mind. It could be **stored** longer than memory, **copied** and moved across distance, and **accumulated** across generations. Knowledge stopped dying with the knower. That's the deep function of every information technology since — the printing press, the telegraph, the computer, the internet — all doing the same three things (store, transmit, accumulate) at ever-greater scale.

sections.label: It also created power
sections.body: Whoever could write could **administer**: levy taxes, enforce contracts, issue laws, and run a bureaucracy larger than any chief could hold in his head. Writing and the **state** grew up together — which is why literacy was long guarded by a small scribe class. Control of information has meant power from the very first tablet, a thread we'll follow through the printing press and beyond.

sections.caption: The origins of writing and the birth of cuneiform — how record-keeping became a full script.

takeaways: The earliest writing was **accounting** — records of grain, livestock, and taxes, not literature.
It arose to **manage surplus-driven information** that had outgrown human memory (builds on the farming lesson).
It evolved tokens → marks → **cuneiform**, and was **independently invented** in several civilizations.
Only later did symbols represent **sounds**, letting writing capture anything language could.
Writing lets knowledge be **stored, copied, and accumulated** — the same job every later info technology does — and it concentrated **power** in those who controlled it.

quiz.q: What was most of the world's earliest writing actually used for?
options: Accounting — tracking goods, debts, and taxes
quiz.explain: The oldest tablets are overwhelmingly economic records. Writing was born to manage the information that farming's surplus created.

quiz.q: What was the key later step that let writing capture anything language could?
options: Symbols coming to represent sounds, not just objects/quantities
quiz.explain: Once signs stood for sounds (not just things and numbers), writing could record names, laws, and stories — anything speakable.

quiz.q: According to the lesson, what three things does every information technology (writing, print, the internet) fundamentally do?
quiz.explain: Writing let knowledge be stored beyond memory, copied across distance, and accumulated over generations — the same core functions later technologies scaled up.
